read_this_first: The question: 'done once, learned'. Where can that be true on real projects? Where a project makes one change in many files. One changed file is the example; how much of what the developers did to the other files does it give?

15 merged pull requests of other people's projects, found by eight title phrases; 89 changed files. Every file in turn is the example and every other drawn file of its pull request is edited: 440 askings. The organ is canonical/swe_kernel/taught_actions/edit_by_example_v1.py, as it stands in the tree.

One example: the organ edited in 142 of 440 askings and made 388 of the developers' 1674 changes (23 in 100). The middle pull request: 20 in 100. In 2 of 15 pull requests one example gave 90 in 100 or more; in 5 it gave nothing.

What it changes is nearly always what the developers did: 396 of its 409 changes (97 in 100). Of the other 13, 12 are at a line the developers changed further than the organ did, and 1 is an import line the developers left alone.
Two examples: 1089 of 3326 (33 in 100); 1118 of its 1150 changes are the developers'.
An example of another kind of change: the organ edited in 7 of 1163 askings; none of its 19 changes there is one the developers made.

By kind of change, from one example: a renamed method or a call written the old way, 38 to 58 in 100; a call no longer to be used, 30; types written another way, 7; text put together as f-strings, 0; a library taken out, 0. Every f-string is another expression and taking a library out removes whole lines: the organ learns the changed expression of its example and repeats that expression.
In 24 of the 89 files the organ can learn nothing from the file's own change: the change is only import lines (12), or it adds, removes or reshapes whole statements.

No test was run: agreement with the developers is the measure. This is the best case by construction, because the pull requests were looked for as repeats of one change. One run by the producer on one machine; nobody else has run it. Zero model calls.

limits: One machine, one producer, one run. Nobody else has run this.

The eight title phrases were chosen by the producer, who had seen the titles of the first eight results of each before fixing them. No pull request had been opened or put to the organ then, and none of the eight phrases was dropped afterwards.
GitHub's search order changes with time. The record names every pull request, the two commits and the hash of every file text, so the same files can be fetched again.

Only files Python 3.11 reads before and after, at most 100,000 bytes, six drawn by a seed from each pull request. A pull request with fewer than six changed Python files, or fewer than four usable ones, was passed over.

A line the organ changed only in part counts against it as a change the developers did not make. A run of lines the developers replaced by a run of another length is one change, and the organ gets no credit for a part of it.
No test was run. A change the developers did not make may be harmless; one they made may be wrong.
Fifteen pull requests, one or two for each kind of change: the numbers by kind are of two pull requests each.
The organ belongs to another session of this project. It was measured as it stands and nothing in it was changed.
This says how far one example reaches inside a change that is repeated. It does not say how much of software work is of that kind.
